bits.title: Bits and bytes
bits.summary: Learn why computers use only 0 and 1, and how bits form bytes and numbers.
bits.lesson.0: A computer stores everything as numbers: text, pictures, music and also programs. Inside the computer, each number is made of tiny switches that are either off or on. We write off as `0` and on as `1`.
bits.lesson.1: One such `0` or `1` is a **bit** (short for binary digit). Computers use only two states because a circuit can tell "no voltage" and "voltage" apart quickly and reliably, even when the signal is not perfect.
bits.lesson.3: Numbers made of bits are **binary** numbers. In decimal, each place is worth 10 times the place to its right: 1, 10, 100. In binary, each place is worth 2 times more: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. To read a binary number, add the values of the places that hold a `1`. So `1101` is 8 + 4 + 1 = 13.
bits.lesson.4: This course uses short Python programs to check numbers. The output below each program is what it prints. `print(...)` shows a value, always in decimal. A number that starts with `0b` is written in binary, and `bin(n)` shows the number `n` in binary.
bits.lesson.7: A group of 8 bits is a **byte**. A byte is the smallest unit that a computer reads or writes in memory. Its value goes from `00000000` (0) to `11111111` (255). `format(n, "08b")` shows `n` as 8 binary digits, with zeros in front.
bits.lesson.9: Every extra bit doubles the number of values. With `n` bits you get 2 to the power of `n` different values. In Python, `**` means "to the power of", so `2 ** 8` is 2 multiplied by itself 8 times.
bits.lesson.11: One byte has 256 different values, but they are 0 to 255, because counting starts at 0. This is why the number 255 shows up so often in computing.
bits.lesson.12: Memory is a long row of bytes. Each byte has a number, its **address**, starting at 0. A program is also a row of bytes in memory. In this course you learn to read those bytes the way the **CPU** (the processor) does.
bits.card.0: A **bit** is `0` or `1`; a **byte** is 8 bits
bits.card.3: `n` bits give `2 ** n` values; a byte holds `0` to `255`
bits-2.explain: 6 is 4 + 2, so the places 4 and 2 hold a `1`: `110`.
bits-3.prompt: How many bits are in one byte?
bits-3.explain: A byte is a group of 8 bits.
bits-4.explain: All 8 places hold a `1`: 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255. `print` shows it in decimal.
bits-5.statement: With 4 bits you can write 16 different values.
bits-5.explain: `2 ** 4` is 16: the values 0 to 15, from `0000` to `1111`.
bits-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `00001001`.
bits-6.explain: `08b` means binary with 8 digits and zeros in front. `8b` fills with spaces, `b` adds nothing, and `d` is decimal.
bits-7.prompt: Build a line that prints how many different values one byte can hold.
bits-7.explain: A byte has 8 bits, so it holds `2 ** 8` = 256 different values.
bits-8.prompt: Put the numbers in order from smallest to largest.
bits-9.prompt: Match the binary number with its value.
bits-10.prompt: One comment shows the wrong result. Which line is it?
bits-11.prompt: How many different values can 3 bits hold?
bits-11.explain: `2 ** 3` is 8: the values `000` to `111`, which are 0 to 7.
bits-12.explain: `print` shows numbers in decimal, so it prints `8`. Only `bin(8)` gives `0b1000`.
hex.title: Hexadecimal
hex.summary: Write every byte as two hex digits and convert between hex, binary and decimal.
hex.lesson.0: Binary numbers get long fast: the byte 200 is `11001000`. This is why programmers write bytes in **hexadecimal** (hex for short), a number system with 16 digits.
hex.lesson.1: Hex uses the digits `0` to `9` and then the letters `A` to `F` for the values 10 to 15. Each place is worth 16 times the place to its right: 1, 16, 256 and so on. So hex `2A` is 2 × 16 + 10 = 42.
hex.lesson.2: To show that a number is hex, write `0x` in front of it: `0x2A`. Python understands this notation. `hex(n)` shows a number in hex, and `int("C3", 16)` reads the text `C3` as a hex number. Python writes the letters in lowercase, but `0x2A` and `0x2a` are the same number.
hex.lesson.4: One hex digit is four bits
hex.lesson.5: One hex digit has 16 values, the same as 4 bits (`2 ** 4` is 16). So every hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits, and every byte is exactly two hex digits. To convert a byte from hex to binary, convert each digit on its own: `C` is `1100` and `3` is `0011`, so `0xC3` is `11000011`.
hex.lesson.7: `format(n, "02X")` shows `n` as two hex digits, with capital letters and a zero in front if needed. This is the usual way to write a byte.
hex.lesson.10: A row of bytes is usually written as hex pairs with spaces, like `48 69 21`. Tools show the contents of files and memory this way. Text is bytes, too: each letter has a number, for example `H` is `0x48`.
hex.lesson.11: In the next program, `data = ...` stores bytes under the name `data`. `bytes.fromhex` turns hex pairs into real bytes, and `list(data)` shows their values in decimal. Python prints bytes that are letters as `b'...'`. `data.hex(" ")` turns the bytes back into hex pairs.
hex.lesson.13: Learn a few values by heart: `0x0F` is 15, `0x10` is 16, `0x7F` is 127, `0x80` is 128 and `0xFF` is 255.
hex.card.0: Hex digits: `0` to `9`, then `A` = 10 up to `F` = 15
hex.card.2: 1 hex digit = 4 bits; 1 byte = 2 hex digits
hex-2.explain: 200 = 12 × 16 + 8. The digit for 12 is `c`, so the result is `0xc8`.
hex-3.explain: `0xFF` is 15 × 16 + 15 = 255, the largest value of one byte. `0x100` is 256.
hex-4.explain: Convert each digit: `A` is `1010` and `5` is `0101`.
hex-5.statement: Every byte can be written with exactly two hex digits.
hex-5.explain: A byte goes from `00` to `FF`, and one hex digit stands for 4 bits.
hex-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `195`.
hex-6.explain: The `16` tells Python to read the text as hex. In the other number systems `C` is not a digit.
hex-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `0A`.
hex-7.explain: `02X` means two hex digits with capital letters and a zero in front. `2X` fills with a space.
hex-8.prompt: Build a line that prints the value of hex `7F` in decimal.
hex-9.prompt: Put the numbers in order from smallest to largest.
hex-10.prompt: Match the hex digit with its bits.
hex-11.prompt: One comment shows the wrong result. Which line is it?
numbers.title: Numbers in memory
numbers.summary: Store big numbers in several bytes, write negative numbers in two's complement and read little-endian bytes.
numbers.lesson.0: One byte only holds 0 to 255. For bigger numbers the CPU uses several bytes together: 2 bytes (16 bits), 4 bytes (32 bits) or 8 bytes (64 bits). A 64-bit CPU like x86-64 works with up to 8 bytes at once.
numbers.lesson.1: A number that can never be negative is **unsigned**. With `n` bits it goes from 0 to `2 ** n - 1`.
numbers.lesson.4: A **signed** number can also be negative. x86-64 uses **two's complement**: to write `-x`, flip every bit of `x` (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0) and add 1. For example, 5 is `00000101`. Flipped, it is `11111010`, and plus 1 gives `11111011`, which is `0xFB`. So the byte `0xFB` means -5.
numbers.lesson.5: In Python, `n & 0xFF` keeps only the lowest 8 bits of `n`. For a negative number this gives exactly its two's complement byte. `& 0xFFFFFFFF` keeps the lowest 32 bits.
numbers.lesson.7: In a signed number, the highest bit shows the sign: `0` means zero or positive, `1` means negative. A signed byte holds -128 to 127. The same byte can mean two things: `0xFF` is 255 unsigned, but -1 signed. The bytes do not say which one is meant; the instruction that uses them decides.
numbers.lesson.8: Two's complement makes adding easy. 255 + 1 does not fit in a byte, so the result wraps around to 0, and -1 + 1 is also 0. The CPU uses the same adding circuit for signed and unsigned numbers.
numbers.lesson.10: A 4-byte number fills 4 addresses in memory. x86-64 stores the **lowest** byte first, at the lowest address. This order is called **little endian**. The number `0x12345678` is stored as the bytes `78 56 34 12`.
numbers.lesson.11: `n.to_bytes(4, "little")` makes the 4 little-endian bytes of `n`, and `int.from_bytes(data, "little")` reads such bytes back. With `signed=True`, Python uses two's complement.
numbers.lesson.13: Little endian reverses the order of the **bytes**, not of the hex digits. `0x1234` is stored as `34 12`, not as `43 21`.
numbers.card.0: Unsigned byte: `0` to `255`; signed byte: `-128` to `127`
numbers.card.1: `-x`: flip all bits of `x`, then add 1
numbers-1.explain: 2 is `00000010`. Flipped it is `11111101`, plus 1 is `11111110`, which is `0xfe`.
numbers-2.prompt: Write the 4 bytes of `0x0A0B0C0D` in little-endian order, as hex pairs.
numbers-2.explain: The lowest byte `0D` comes first, the highest byte `0A` last.
numbers-3.prompt: Which byte means -1 in two's complement?
numbers-4.explain: `0x80` is `10000000`. The highest bit is 1, so as a signed byte it is negative: -128.
numbers-5.statement: In little-endian order, the bytes `34 12` are the number `0x3412`.
numbers-5.explain: The first byte is the lowest one, so `34 12` is `0x1234`.
numbers-6.statement: A signed byte can hold the value 200.
numbers-6.explain: A signed byte holds -128 to 127. Only an unsigned byte can hold 200.
numbers-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `e8 03 00 00`.
numbers-7.explain: `little` puts the lowest byte `e8` first. `big` would give `00 00 03 e8`.
numbers-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `-3`.
numbers-8.explain: With `signed=True` Python reads `0xFD` in two's complement, which is -3. Without it you get 253.
numbers-9.prompt: Build a line that prints the two's complement byte of -6 in hex.
numbers-9.explain: `& 0xFF` keeps the lowest 8 bits, so the line prints `0xfa`.
numbers-10.prompt: Put the bytes of `0x11223344` in the order they are stored in memory, lowest address first.
numbers-10.explain: x86-64 is little endian: the lowest byte `44` comes first.
numbers-11.prompt: Match the byte with its value as a signed byte.
numbers-12.prompt: One comment shows the wrong result. Which line is it?
numbers-12.explain: 4660 is `0x1234`. Little endian puts the low byte first: `34 12`.
instructions.title: Instructions are bytes
instructions.summary: See how the CPU fetches and runs instructions, meet NOP, RET and INT3, and turn assembly into bytes with NASM.
instructions.lesson.0: A program is a row of bytes, too. The CPU reads them as **instructions**: small commands like "add two numbers" or "go to another place". These bytes are called **machine code**. In this course you learn the machine code of **x86-64**, the CPU family of most PCs and servers.
instructions.lesson.1: Each instruction starts with an **opcode**, a byte that says what to do. Some instructions are only this one byte. `0x90` is `NOP` (no operation): it does nothing. `0xC3` is `RET` (return): it ends a function and goes back to the code that called it. `0xCC` is `INT3`, a breakpoint: it stops the program and hands it to a debugger.
instructions.lesson.3: The CPU has a register called **RIP**, the instruction pointer. It holds the address of the next instruction. The CPU repeats a loop again and again: it **fetches** the bytes at RIP, **decodes** them to find out which instruction it is and how long it is, moves RIP forward by that length, and then **executes** the instruction.
instructions.lesson.4: This Python program imitates the decoder for one-byte instructions. `names` is a dictionary: it maps each opcode to its name. The `for` loop repeats the indented line for every byte, and `enumerate` gives each byte together with its address.
instructions.lesson.7: Nobody wants to remember that `0xC3` means return. **Assembly language** gives each instruction a short name, like `nop` or `ret`. A program called an **assembler** turns assembly into machine code. This course uses the assembler **NASM**. The first line, `bits 64`, tells NASM to make x86-64 code.
instructions.lesson.8: For assembly examples, the output shows the bytes that NASM makes, in hex, one line per instruction. You can make them yourself with `nasm -f bin file.asm` and look at the result with a hex viewer. Short examples in the exercises leave out the line `bits 64`.
instructions.lesson.10: With `db` (define byte), you write bytes directly. You can put several bytes on one line, separated by commas. The CPU cannot tell where the bytes came from: `db 0x90` and `nop` give the same byte.
instructions.lesson.12: Bytes have no meaning by themselves. `C3` is `RET` when the CPU runs it, but the number 195 when a program reads it as data. On other CPU families, like ARM, the same bytes are completely different instructions.
instructions.lesson.13: x86-64 instructions are 1 to 15 bytes long. A **disassembler** does the opposite of an assembler: it turns bytes back into assembly, so you can read machine code.
instructions.card.1: The opcode byte says which instruction it is
instructions.card.2: RIP holds the address of the next instruction
instructions.card.3: Fetch, decode, move RIP forward, execute
instructions-1.prompt: What bytes does NASM make for this code?
instructions-2.explain: `C3` is `RET`. `nop` is `90`, `int3` is `CC`, and `db` is not an instruction but tells NASM to write bytes.
instructions-3.prompt: How many instructions are in these bytes?
instructions-3.explain: Each of these opcodes is a whole instruction of one byte: three `nop` and one `ret`.
instructions-4.prompt: RIP is `0x1000`, and the byte there is `90` (`nop`). What is RIP after the CPU has executed it?
instructions-4.explain: `nop` is 1 byte long, so RIP moves forward by 1.
instructions-5.statement: `db 0xC3` and `ret` give the same machine code.
instructions-5.explain: Both make the byte `C3`. The CPU cannot tell how the byte was written.
instructions-6.statement: While an instruction runs, RIP already holds the address of the next instruction.
instructions-6.explain: The CPU moves RIP forward by the length of the instruction before it executes it.
instructions-7.prompt: Complete the code so NASM makes the bytes `90 90 C3`.
instructions-7.explain: `db 0x90` writes the byte `90`. `db 90` is decimal 90, which is the byte `5A`.
instructions-8.prompt: Build a NASM line that writes the bytes `90` and `C3`.
instructions-8.explain: `db` writes the bytes in the given order, separated by commas.
instructions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so NASM makes the bytes `90 CC C3 90 C3`.
instructions-9.explain: `nop` is `90`, `int3` is `CC`, the `db` line writes `C3 90`, and `ret` is `C3`.
instructions-10.prompt: Match the byte with what the instruction does.
instructions-11.prompt: One comment shows the wrong bytes. Which line is it?
instructions-11.explain: Without `0x`, NASM reads `90` as decimal, which is the byte `5A`. Write `db 0x90`.
instructions-12.prompt: The CPU starts at the first byte. How many of these instructions does it run?
instructions-12.explain: It runs two `nop` and then `ret`. `ret` goes back to the caller, so the last `nop` never runs.
registers.title: Registers in machine code
registers.summary: Meet the x86-64 registers and their numbers, and encode MOV with a value as B8 plus the register number.
registers.lesson.0: **Registers** are tiny storage places inside the CPU. They are much faster than memory, so most instructions work with registers. x86-64 has 16 general registers of 64 bits each: `RAX`, `RCX`, `RDX`, `RBX`, `RSP`, `RBP`, `RSI`, `RDI` and `R8` to `R15`.
registers.lesson.1: The lower 32 bits of each register have their own name: `EAX` is the lower half of `RAX`, `ECX` of `RCX`, and so on. This course mostly uses the 32-bit names. When an instruction writes a 32-bit register, the CPU sets the upper 32 bits of the full register to 0.
registers.lesson.3: Inside machine code, a register is not a name but a number from 0 to 7. Note the order: it is A, C, D, B, not A, B, C, D. The program below prints the numbers; `names` is a list (`[...]`) of texts.
registers.lesson.6: `mov eax, 1` puts the value 1 into `EAX`. Its machine code is the opcode `B8` plus the register number, followed by the value as 4 bytes in little-endian order. So `B8` means `EAX`, `B9` means `ECX`, `BA` means `EDX`, and so on up to `BF` for `EDI`. The register is part of the opcode byte.
registers.lesson.8: A value inside an instruction is called an **immediate**. Here it is always 4 bytes long, so every `mov` of this kind is 5 bytes: one opcode byte and four bytes for the value. A negative value is stored in two's complement.
registers.lesson.10: To decode such an instruction, subtract `0xB8` from the opcode to get the register number, and read the next 4 bytes as a little-endian number. In Python, `code[0]` is the first byte, and `code[1:5]` are the bytes at positions 1 to 4.
registers.lesson.12: Because writing `EAX` also clears the upper half of `RAX`, `mov eax, 1` makes the whole of `RAX` equal to 1. NASM even turns `mov rax, 1` into the shorter bytes `B8 01 00 00 00`.
registers.lesson.13: `RSP` (number 4) is the **stack pointer**. It points to the stack, a memory area for return addresses and saved values. Do not use it for ordinary calculations.
registers.card.1: `mov` register, value = `B8` + register number, then 4 value bytes
registers.card.3: Writing `EAX` sets the upper half of `RAX` to 0
registers-1.prompt: What bytes does NASM make for this code?
registers-1.explain: `EDX` is number 2, so the opcode is `B8` + 2 = `BA`. Then come the 4 bytes of 7.
registers-2.explain: The order is `EAX`, `ECX`, `EDX`, `EBX`, `ESP`, `EBP`, `ESI`, `EDI`, starting at 0. So `mov esi` uses the opcode `BE`.
registers-3.explain: `BF` is `B8` + 7, which is `EDI`. The bytes `0A 00 00 00` are little endian for 10.
registers-4.prompt: How many bytes long is `mov ebx, 1`?
registers-4.explain: One opcode byte (`BB`) and four bytes for the value.
registers-5.statement: In machine code, register number 1 is `EBX`.
registers-6.statement: NASM makes the bytes `B8 00 01 00 00` for this code.
registers-7.prompt: Complete the bytes so they mean `mov ecx, 3`.
registers-7.explain: `ECX` is number 1, so the opcode is `B8` + 1 = `B9`.
registers-8.prompt: Complete the code so NASM makes the bytes `B8 FF FF FF FF`.
registers-8.explain: -1 in two's complement has all bits set. 255 would give `FF 00 00 00`.
registers-9.explain: `EBX` gives the opcode `BB`. The value `0x00000102` is stored lowest byte first: `02 01 00 00`.
registers-10.prompt: Put the bytes in order so they mean `mov edx, 0x11223344`.
registers-10.explain: First the opcode `BA` (`B8` + 2 for `EDX`), then the value in little-endian order.
registers-11.prompt: Match the opcode with what it does.
registers-12.prompt: One comment shows the wrong bytes. Which line is it?
registers-12.explain: `EBX` is number 3, so the opcode is `B8` + 3 = `BB`. `BA` is `EDX`.
arithmetic.title: Arithmetic instructions
arithmetic.summary: Encode ADD, SUB, INC and DEC, and learn how the ModR/M byte names the registers.
arithmetic.lesson.0: `add eax, ecx` adds `ECX` to `EAX` and stores the result in `EAX`. `sub eax, ecx` subtracts `ECX` from `EAX`. The first register is the **destination**: it receives the result. The second one is the **source**.
arithmetic.lesson.1: These instructions are 2 bytes long. The first byte is the opcode: `01` for `ADD` and `29` for `SUB`. The second byte is the **ModR/M** byte. It names the two registers.
arithmetic.lesson.4: The 8 bits of ModR/M have three fields: `mod` (2 bits), `reg` (3 bits) and `rm` (3 bits). `mod` = `11` means that both operands are registers. Here `reg` holds the source register and `rm` the destination register.
arithmetic.lesson.5: For `add eax, ecx` the source is `ECX` (number 1, `001`) and the destination is `EAX` (number 0, `000`). So ModR/M is `11` `001` `000`, which is `0xC8`. In Python you can put `_` between the fields of a binary number; the `_` only makes it easier to read.
arithmetic.lesson.7: `DA` is the ModR/M byte of `sub edx, ebx`: the source `EBX` is `011` and the destination `EDX` is `010`. `C1` has the source `EAX` and the destination `ECX`, so `01 C1` is `add ecx, eax`.
arithmetic.lesson.9: `add ecx, 5` adds a value to a register. For values from -128 to 127 the opcode is `83`, then a ModR/M byte, then the value as one signed byte. Here the `reg` field holds no register but a number that picks the operation: `0` for ADD and `5` for SUB. So `add ecx, 5` has ModR/M `11` `000` `001` = `C1`, and `sub ecx, 2` has `11` `101` `001` = `E9`.
arithmetic.lesson.11: `inc ecx` adds 1 and `dec ecx` subtracts 1. Both use the opcode `FF` and a ModR/M byte, with `0` in the `reg` field for INC and `1` for DEC. So `inc ecx` is `FF C1` and `dec ecx` is `FF C9`.
arithmetic.lesson.13: In 64-bit code you often see the byte `48` in front of an instruction. It is a **prefix** that makes the instruction work with all 64 bits: `add rax, rcx` is `48 01 C8`.
arithmetic-1.prompt: What bytes does NASM make for this code?
arithmetic-1.explain: The source `EDX` is `010` and the destination `EBX` is `011`, so ModR/M is `11` `010` `011` = `D3`.
arithmetic-2.prompt: Which value is in `EAX` after these instructions run?
arithmetic-3.explain: `29` is SUB. ModR/M `C8` is `11` `001` `000`: the source is `ECX` and the destination is `EAX`.
arithmetic-4.prompt: What is the ModR/M byte of `add edx, ecx`?
arithmetic-4.explain: The source `ECX` goes into `reg` (`001`) and the destination `EDX` into `rm` (`010`): `11` `001` `010` = `CA`.
arithmetic-5.statement: `inc eax` and `add eax, 1` have the same machine code.
arithmetic-5.explain: Both add 1, but `inc eax` is `FF C0` and `add eax, 1` is `83 C0 01`.
arithmetic-6.statement: NASM makes the bytes `FF CB` for this code.
arithmetic-6.explain: DEC uses `1` in the `reg` field, and `EBX` is `011`: `11` `001` `011` = `CB`.
arithmetic-7.prompt: Complete the bytes so they mean `add eax, 3`.
arithmetic-7.explain: ADD uses `0` in the `reg` field and `EAX` is `000`, so ModR/M is `11` `000` `000` = `C0`. `E8` would be SUB.
arithmetic-8.prompt: Complete the code so NASM makes the bytes `29 D9`.
arithmetic-8.explain: `D9` is `11` `011` `001`: the source is `EBX` (`011`) and the destination is `ECX` (`001`).
arithmetic-9.prompt: Build the instruction for the bytes `29 D1`.
arithmetic-9.explain: `29` is SUB. `D1` is `11` `010` `001`: the source `EDX`, the destination `ECX`.
arithmetic-10.prompt: Put the instructions in order so `EAX` ends with the value 7.
arithmetic-10.explain: 3 - 1 is 2, doubled is 4, plus 3 is 7. Every other order gives a different result.
arithmetic-11.prompt: Match the bytes with what they do.
arithmetic-12.prompt: One comment shows the wrong bytes. Which line is it?
arithmetic-12.explain: DEC uses `1` in the `reg` field: `11` `001` `001` = `C9`, so `dec ecx` is `FF C9`.
jumps.title: Jumps and offsets
jumps.summary: Jump forward and back with short jumps, compute relative offsets, and make decisions with conditional jumps.
jumps.lesson.0: Normally the CPU runs one instruction after the other. A **jump** changes RIP, so the CPU goes on somewhere else. Jumps make loops and decisions possible.
jumps.lesson.1: The short jump `JMP` is 2 bytes: the opcode `EB` and one signed byte, the **offset**. The offset says how far to jump, counted from the address **after** the jump instruction. A positive offset jumps forward, a negative one jumps back.
jumps.lesson.2: In NASM you jump to a **label**: a name followed by `:` that marks an address. NASM computes the offset for you. Below, the jump is at address 0 and ends at address 2. The label `skip` is at address 4, so the offset is 4 - 2 = 2, and the CPU skips the two `nop` bytes.
jumps.lesson.5: The rule for every offset is: offset = target address - address after the jump. To jump back, the offset is negative and written in two's complement. In NASM, `$` means the address of the current instruction, so `jmp $` jumps to itself, forever. Its offset is 0 - 2 = -2, which is the byte `FE`.
jumps.lesson.7: Python can compute the offset byte: subtract, then keep the lowest byte with `& 0xFF`. The three lines compute the offsets of `jmp skip`, of `jmp $` and of a jump from address 9 back to address 5.
jumps.lesson.10: A **conditional jump** jumps only if a condition is true; otherwise the CPU goes on with the next instruction. The condition comes from the **flags**: single bits that arithmetic instructions set. For example, the **zero flag** is 1 when a result is 0. `cmp eax, ebx` compares two registers: it subtracts `EBX` from `EAX`, sets the flags and throws the result away.
jumps.lesson.11: Short conditional jumps are 2 bytes: an opcode from `70` to `7F` and an offset. Common ones are `74` = `JZ` (jump if zero, also called `JE`, jump if equal), `75` = `JNZ` (jump if not zero, `JNE`), `7C` = `JL` (jump if less) and `7F` = `JG` (jump if greater). This loop repeats `dec ecx` until `ECX` is 0. The jump ends at address 9 and goes back to address 5, so the offset is -4 = `FC`.
jumps.lesson.13: A short offset reaches from -128 to 127 bytes. For longer jumps, NASM uses the near form with a 4-byte offset: `E9` for `JMP`, or `0F 84` for `JZ`.
jumps.card.1: offset = target - address after the jump
jumps.card.4: `cmp eax, ebx` sets the flags like `sub` but keeps no result
jumps-1.prompt: A `jmp` at address `0x10` has the bytes `EB 05`. To which address does it jump? Answer in hex with `0x`.
jumps-2.prompt: What bytes does NASM make for this code?
jumps-2.explain: The jump ends at address 2 and `done` is at address 3, so the offset is 1.
jumps-3.prompt: A jump ends at address 20, and its target is address 16. Which offset byte does it need?
jumps-4.options.0: It jumps 3 bytes forward if the zero flag is 1.
jumps-4.options.2: It jumps 3 bytes forward if the zero flag is 0.
jumps-4.explain: `74` is `JZ`: it jumps only when the zero flag is 1. The offset 3 counts from the end of the instruction.
jumps-5.statement: The offset of a short jump is counted from the first byte of the jump instruction.
jumps-5.explain: It is counted from the address after the jump, the place where the CPU would go on without jumping.
jumps-6.prompt: Which value is in `EAX` when the code reaches `ret`?
jumps-6.explain: The loop runs 4 times, because `ECX` goes 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. Each time `EAX` grows by 2.
jumps-7.prompt: Complete the code so the loop runs exactly 5 times.
jumps-7.explain: `jnz` jumps back while `ECX` is not 0. `jz` and `jl` stop after one round, and `jmp` never stops.
jumps-8.prompt: Complete the bytes so the jump goes to itself.
jumps-8.explain: The jump is 2 bytes long, so it must go back 2 bytes: -2 = `FE`. `00` goes on with the next instruction.
jumps-9.prompt: Build the bytes of `dec ecx`, followed by a `jnz` that jumps back to `dec ecx`.
jumps-9.explain: `dec ecx` is `FF C9`. The `jnz` (`75`) ends 4 bytes after the start of `dec ecx`, so the offset is -4 = `FC`.
jumps-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so NASM makes the bytes `B9 02 00 00 00 FF C9 75 FC C3`.
jumps-10.explain: The offset `FC` (-4) only fits when `again:` marks `dec ecx`.
jumps-11.prompt: Match the opcode with the jump.
jumps-12.prompt: One comment shows the wrong bytes. Which line is it?
jumps-12.explain: The jump ends at address 9 and `again` is at address 5: 5 - 9 = -4 = `FC`. `FE` would jump to the `jnz` itself.
programs.title: A whole program
programs.summary: Call the operating system with syscall, write a complete program as bytes, and read hex dumps and disassembly.
programs.lesson.0: A program cannot print text or stop by itself: it asks the operating system. On Linux, x86-64 programs do this with a **system call**. The instruction `syscall` has the 2 bytes `0F 05`.
programs.lesson.1: Before `syscall`, the program puts the number of the system call into `EAX` and the arguments into `EDI`, `ESI` and `EDX`, or into `RDI`, `RSI` and `RDX` for big values like addresses. Two useful numbers: `60` is `exit` (stop the program, with the exit code in `EDI`) and `1` is `write` (write bytes).
programs.lesson.2: This is a complete Linux program. It puts 60 into `EAX` and the exit code 42 into `EDI`, and then calls the operating system. The output shows its 12 bytes.
programs.lesson.4: When these 12 bytes run on Linux, the program stops at once with the exit code 42. In a terminal, `echo $?` then shows `42`. To run, the bytes must be inside an executable file, which NASM and the linker `ld` can make. The operating system loads the bytes into memory and sets RIP to the first one.
programs.lesson.6: The `write` system call needs three arguments: where to write in `EDI` (1 means the screen, called standard output), the address of the bytes in `RSI`, and how many bytes in `EDX`. `lea rsi, [rel msg]` puts the address of the label `msg` into `RSI`. `xor edi, edi` is a short way to set `EDI` to 0.
programs.lesson.7: `db "Hi", 10` writes the letters `H` and `i` and the byte 10, which starts a new line. This time the output is not the bytes but what the program prints when it runs.
programs.lesson.10: A **hex dump** shows the bytes of a file. The tool `xxd` prints the address of the first byte of each line, then 16 bytes in hex (in groups of two), then the same bytes as text, with a dot for each byte that is not a letter. This is the hex dump of the program above:
programs.lesson.12: A **disassembler** turns the bytes back into assembly. `ndisasm -b 64` (it comes with NASM) prints the address, the bytes and the instruction on each line. The last three bytes are the text `Hi` and the new line, but the disassembler does not know that, so it tries to read them as instructions.
programs-1.prompt: In this hex dump, which byte is at address `0x05`?
programs-1.explain: Each pair of hex digits is one byte, starting with address 0: `b8 3c 00 00 00 bf`. So address 5 holds `bf`.
programs-2.prompt: With which exit code does this program stop?
programs-2.explain: `B8 3C 00 00 00` puts 60 (`exit`) into `EAX`, `BF 07 00 00 00` puts 7 into `EDI`, and `0F 05` is `syscall`.
programs-3.prompt: Which value must be in `EAX` for the `exit` system call?
programs-3.explain: 60 is the number of `exit` on Linux x86-64. 1 is `write`, and 42 was only an exit code.
programs-4.explain: `EDX` says how many bytes to write: 2, so only `O` and `K` appear.
programs-5.explain: XOR of a value with itself is always 0. It is a short way to clear a register (2 bytes instead of 5).
programs-6.statement: This program stops with the exit code 0.
programs-6.explain: The order of the two `mov` instructions does not matter. When `syscall` runs, `EAX` is 60 and `EDI` is 0.
programs-7.prompt: Complete the program so it stops with the exit code 3.
programs-7.explain: `EAX` holds the number of the system call, and `exit` is 60. `0x60` is 96.
programs-8.prompt: Complete the bytes so the program stops with the exit code 1.
programs-8.explain: `BF` is `mov edi`, and the value 1 in little endian is `01 00 00 00`.
programs-9.prompt: Build the bytes of `mov eax, 60`, then `xor edi, edi`, then `syscall`.
programs-9.explain: `mov eax, 60` is `B8 3C 00 00 00`, `xor edi, edi` is `31 FF` and `syscall` is `0F 05`.
programs-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so NASM makes the bytes `31 FF B8 3C 00 00 00 FF C7 0F 05`.
programs-10.explain: `31 FF` is `xor edi, edi`, `B8 3C 00 00 00` is `mov eax, 60`, `FF C7` is `inc edi` and `0F 05` is `syscall`.
programs-11.prompt: Match the bytes with their meaning.
programs-12.prompt: This program should print `Hi` and a new line. Which line has the bug?
programs-12.explain: The text has 3 bytes: `H`, `i` and the new line. Write `mov edx, 3`.
